paras: The lynching of Amos Miller was the hanging of a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Scott, a white woman of Maury County, Tennessee, by an armed mob that seized him in the court room at Franklin, Williamson County, on August 10, 1888. About fifty unmasked men took Miller while his lawyers sought a delay in his trial and hanged him from a railing of the court house in the presence of the court. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown parties.

Miller, described as about twenty-one, was charged with criminally assaulting Mrs. Scott in June 1888; one early report called him "Thomas Davis, a negro of very bad reputation, who is known also as Amos Miller." Arrested at Santa Fe, Maury County, he was jailed at Columbia, where, according to the Atlanta Constitution and the Memphis Appeal, he admitted the act.

When the Maury County sheriff learned that a mob was coming to the Columbia jail, he moved Miller to Franklin. Warned that seventy-five to one hundred men were on their way there, Sheriff Russell of Williamson County and the jailer hid Miller in a wheat field outside town overnight and then took him by train to Nashville. The mob searched every cell of the Franklin jail, waited two hours, and dispersed.

Court officers arranged a special session at Franklin, and on the morning of August 10 Miller was brought from Nashville and arraigned. According to the Memphis Appeal's Franklin correspondent, the mob had promised to make no demonstration if he were tried at once, but it stood organized and waiting for its leaders' signal. When defense lawyers House and Henderson applied for a continuance and prepared to seek a change of venue, word reached the mob.

At about 10:30 a.m. an "organized body of about fifty men, well armed" entered the court room, seized Miller, and hanged him almost in the presence of the judge. An effort to dissuade the lynchers failed, and, in the Appeal's words, "No one was allowed to interfere." Miller's brother watched the hanging without protest, and the mob, none of them disguised, dispersed quietly.

The coroner's jury returned a verdict of death at the hands of unknown parties, "notwithstanding the fact that not one of the mob was disguised," as the Savannah Courier put it. The Appeal reported "intense excitement" in the county but called the result "nothing more than was expected" by many. No report of arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Every account comes from white newspapers, which treated the accusation as fact. The Memphis Appeal ran its Franklin dispatch on its front page under headlines calling Miller a "Villain" and declaring that "The Story of His Crime Retold Almost Justifies This Disregard for the Law."

Two Nashville wire versions spread the news on August 11. The shorter, one sentence about fifty armed men and a balcony, ran in papers from Washington to Salt Lake City under heads such as "Lynched in Broad Daylight" and "A Ravisher Lynched." The longer, carried by the Maysville Evening Bulletin, the Rock Island Daily Argus and the Big Sandy News, added the unmasked mob and the inquest verdict under heads such as "Judge Lynch Reports Business."

In the South, the Atlanta Constitution headed its item "Tennessee Justice," and the Pulaski Citizen called Miller "the raplst." The Savannah Courier, like the long wire, set the inquest's finding against the open conduct of the mob, while weekly digests as far off as Dakota reduced the lynching to a line.

Accounts differ on where Miller was hanged: a banister rail or railing inside the building in the Appeal and the Pulaski Citizen, a balcony in the short wire, and the front-porch railing in the long wire. The Alexandria Gazette alone said he was taken "from jail." The Appeal put the mob at "about fifty," the Savannah Courier at "a small mob."

The alleged assault was dated June 10 by the Appeal and the Courier and June 15 by the long wire, which also placed it in Williamson rather than Maury County. The National Tribune gave the day of the lynching as Saturday rather than Friday.
